prompt.brief: Design a weather service that aggregates provider observations and forecasts, serves current conditions and multi-day outlooks, and delivers timely location-aware alerts with freshness metadata.
successSignals: Define provider normalization, station/grid identity, forecast versions, units, timezone, freshness, confidence, and alert lifecycle.
Cache by geospatial cell and forecast horizon, refresh adaptively, reconcile conflicting providers, and avoid thundering-herd refreshes.
Separate provider ingestion from serving projections, historical observations, notifications, and expensive forecast transformations.
Explain provider outage, stale labeling, alert deduplication, location privacy, observability, and degraded cached forecasts.

functional: Return current conditions, hourly/daily forecasts, historical observations, air-quality fields, units, and provider/freshness metadata.
Subscribe users to threshold/severe-weather alerts by location, deduplicate notifications, and support locale/timezone preferences.
Ingest multiple providers, retry safely, backfill gaps, invalidate outdated forecasts, and serve cached data with an explicit stale marker.
nonFunctional: Serve common forecast reads with p95 under 200ms and propagate severe alerts within two minutes of provider receipt.
Scale to 50M users and highly skewed popular locations without a single hot key or unbounded synchronous work.
Do not lose committed state; make retries and duplicate events safe.
Degrade safely when downstream workers, caches, or external dependencies fail.
scaleAssumptions: 50M users, 10M watched locations, and 1M provider updates per hour
Partition by the primary tenant, user, item, or geographic key and isolate hot partitions.
Keep serving state bounded; retain raw events or durable records for replay and auditing.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the Weather service commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional Weather service writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return Weather service version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition Weather service by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound Weather service work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for Weather service projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable Weather service projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable Weather service records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure Weather service latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.
